title: Code Smells
body:
A code smell is **a surface symptom that the design underneath is wrong**. It is not a bug.
The code compiles, the tests pass, the behaviour is correct, and it is still telling you
something. That is the whole reason the word exists: the things that hurt most over a
system's life are not defects, and no test will report them.

## The usual ones

| Smell | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| **Long method** | the method is doing several things: low cohesion |
| **Large class** | same, one level up: the class has more than one responsibility |
| **Duplicated code** | an abstraction exists and has not been named |
| **Long parameter list** | passing state that should be an object, or stamp coupling |
| **Feature envy** | a method uses another class's data more than its own: it is in the wrong class |
| **Shotgun surgery** | one change forces edits in many places: high coupling |
| **Divergent change** | one class changes for many unrelated reasons: low cohesion |
| **Data class** | fields with getters and setters and no behaviour: data and operations got separated |
| **Magic numbers** | a meaning that was never given a name |
| **Long `if`/`switch` on type** | a missing [[Polymorphism|polymorphic]] call |

Read down that right-hand column and it is the same two words every time. Almost every smell
is a [[Coupling and Cohesion]] failure, which is why that note is the one to actually learn.

## How to use them

They are heuristics, not rules. A long method in a parser may be fine; a three-line method
may still be in the wrong class. The value of the list is that it gives a name to a vague
feeling, which makes it arguable in a [[Review]] instead of a matter of taste.

The response to a smell is refactoring: changing structure without changing behaviour, which
is only safe if [[Unit testing]] is there to prove the behaviour did not change. The vault has
no refactoring note; it was not covered as its own topic in this course.

Related: [[Complexity]], [[Metrics]], [[Design]].
